<details class="topic-card" open>
<summary>Fit a simple linear regression with lm()</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Use `lm()` to model a linear relationship between predictor values (`x`) and response values (`y`).

Model form:

$$
y = ax + b
$$

- $a$: slope (how much `y` changes when `x` increases by 1)
- $b$: intercept (predicted `y` when `x = 0`)

In R, that same model is written as `y ~ x` inside `lm()`.

- Left side of `~`: response variable (`y`)
- Right side of `~`: predictor variable (`x`)

So `lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)` means:
"Model absorbance as a linear function of concentration."

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

# Print a short model summary (coefficients)
coef(model)
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Extract slope and intercept with coef()</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

`coef(model)` returns the estimated coefficients as a small vector.

For a simple model `y ~ x`, indexing works like this:

- `coefs[[1]]`: intercept (`b` in `y = ax + b`)
- `coefs[[2]]`: slope (`a` in `y = ax + b`)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why use `[[ ]]` here?
`coef(model)` returns a named vector (for example with names like `(Intercept)` and `conc_ug_ml`).

- `coefs[1]` returns a vector of length 1 (still a vector, with its name attached)
- `coefs[[1]]` returns the single numeric value only

Here we use `[[ ]]` because we want the plain number for calculations and `cat()` output.
:::

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

# Store the coefficient vector once
coefs <- coef(model)

# Index 1 = intercept (b), index 2 = slope (a)
intercept <- coefs[[1]]
slope <- coefs[[2]]

cat("Intercept:", signif(intercept, 4), "\n")
cat("Slope:    ", signif(slope, 4), "\n")
```



</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Use summary() and extract R^2^</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

R^2^, used to interpret goodness of fit, can be assessed from `summary(model)` and extracted as `$r.squared`.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)
model_summary <- summary(model)

# Extract R-squared directly
r2 <- model_summary$r.squared
cat("R-squared:", signif(r2, 4), "\n")
```

If you run `summary(model)` and scroll through the output, you also get:

- Residuals (differences between observed and predicted values)
- Coefficients table (estimate, standard error, t value, p-value)
- Residual standard error
- Adjusted R^2^
- F-statistic

For full output, run:

```{webr}
# Optional: print the full regression report
summary(model)
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Force the regression through (0,0)</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

If your scientific model requires zero intercept, fit without an intercept term.

Equivalent formulas:

- `y ~ 0 + x`
- `y ~ x - 1`

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model_free <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)
model_zero <- lm(absorbance ~ 0 + conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

cat("Free intercept model coefficients:\n")
print(coef(model_free))

cat("\nZero-intercept model coefficient:\n")
print(coef(model_zero))
```

::: {.callout-note}
Use a forced-zero model only when it is scientifically justified. Otherwise, it can bias slope estimates.
:::

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Fit separate regressions for each group with group_by()</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Sometimes one regression line isn't appropriate for the whole data set — for example, if you ran calibration curves for three different compounds and want to check each one's line separately. `group_by()` combined with `summarise()` lets you fit a separate `lm()` model per compound and pull out coefficients and R² for each, in one step.

The tricky part is that `lm()` normally expects a named data frame to point to with `data = ...`. Inside `summarise()`, there isn't one — you're working through the data group by group, not from an existing table. `pick(everything())` solves this: it reassembles the current group's columns into a small data frame on the spot, so `lm()` has something to fit. Since `lm()` returns a whole model object rather than a single number, it's wrapped in `list()` so it can be stored in a single table cell; `model[[1]]` then unwraps that list to get the actual model back out, so `coef()` and `summary()` can work on it.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration_compounds <- tibble(
  compound = rep(c("Compound 1", "Compound 2", "Compound 3"), each = 6),
  conc_ug_ml = rep(c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0), times = 3),
  absorbance = c(
    0.004, 0.058, 0.112, 0.229, 0.438, 0.885,   # Compound 1
    0.002, 0.061, 0.105, 0.223, 0.446, 0.895,   # Compound 2
    0.006, 0.052, 0.118, 0.233, 0.430, 0.870    # Compound 3
  )
)

calibration_compounds %>%
  group_by(compound) %>%
  summarise(
    # Fit one lm() per compound, using just that compound's rows
    model = list(lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = pick(everything()))),

    # Pull out slope, intercept, and R-squared for this compound's model
    intercept = coef(model[[1]])[[1]],
    slope = coef(model[[1]])[[2]],
    r_squared = summary(model[[1]])$r.squared
  ) %>%
  select(-model)   # model column was only needed to get the numbers above
```

The result is one row per compound, with its own slope, intercept, and R², all pulled out using the same `coef()` and `summary()` from earlier on this page — just applied automatically to each group instead of repeating the code three times by hand.

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Predict new values with the regression model</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

## Standard approach: use `predict()` directly

In general, if you have new predictor values (`x`) and want predicted response values (`y`), use `predict()` directly.

If your model is `absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml`, that means:

- input: new concentration values
- output: predicted absorbance values

Rather than calculating the predictions separately and joining them back on afterwards, you can do it in one step with `mutate()`. Inside the pipe, `.` refers to `new_conc` itself as it flows through — so `predict(model, newdata = .)` tells `predict()` to use these new concentration values, and `mutate()` adds the result directly as a new column.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

new_conc <- tibble(conc_ug_ml = c(7.5, 15, 30))

new_conc %>%
  mutate(pred_absorbance = predict(model, newdata = .))
```

## Going the other way: estimating x from new y values

The opposite direction can also be useful: if you have new response values (`y`) and want the corresponding predictor values (`x`).

In calibration work, this is common: you measure absorbance (response, `y`) and want concentration (predictor, `x`).

Because the fitted model is still `absorbance ~ concentration`, estimate concentration by rearranging the fitted line:

$$
  concentration = \frac{\text{absorbance} - b}{a}
$$

where `a` is slope and `b` is intercept.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

# Extract slope (a) and intercept (b)
coefs <- coef(model)
b <- coefs[[1]]
a <- coefs[[2]]

# New absorbance readings from samples
new_abs <- tibble(absorbance = c(0.180, 0.320, 0.750))

# Estimate concentrations from absorbance
new_abs %>%
  mutate(pred_conc_ug_ml = (absorbance - b) / a)
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Plot the regression with geom_smooth() and geom_abline()</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` fits and draws the line directly.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

ggplot(calibration, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#3C5E3E") +
  labs(
    title = "Calibration Data with Linear Fit",
    x = "Concentration (ug/mL)",
    y = "Absorbance"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

Use `geom_abline()` if you want to draw a line from known coefficients.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

intercept <- coef(model)[[1]]
slope <- coef(model)[[2]]

ggplot(calibration, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = "#8B3A3A", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Calibration Data with geom_abline()",
    x = "Concentration (ug/mL)",
    y = "Absorbance"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Annotate equation and R^2^ &nbsp;on the plot</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

You can extract slope/intercept and R^2^, print them with `cat()`, and also place them on the plot.

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

# Pull out fitted line parameters and goodness-of-fit
intercept <- coef(model)[[1]]
slope <- coef(model)[[2]]
r2 <- summary(model)$r.squared

# Build text strings that will be shown on the plot
eq_label <- paste("y =", signif(intercept, 4), "+", signif(slope, 4), "x")
r2_label <- paste("R2 =", signif(r2, 4))

# Also print equation and R2 in the console
cat("Equation:", eq_label, "\n")
cat("R2:", signif(r2, 4), "\n")

ggplot(calibration, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = "#3C5E3E", linewidth = 1) +
  # Add equation and R2 text labels onto the figure
  annotate("text", x = 26, y = 0.35, label = eq_label, hjust = 0, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 26, y = 0.27, label = r2_label, hjust = 0, size = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Linear Regression with Equation and R2",
    x = "Concentration (ug/mL)",
    y = "Absorbance"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Quick quality checks and common pitfalls</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Simple linear regression works best when:

- The relationship is approximately linear
- Residual spread is reasonably constant
- Outliers are checked and justified
- Predictions are mainly within the measured range

How to use the diagnostic plot (`plot(model, which = 1)`):

- X-axis: fitted values (predicted absorbance)
- Y-axis: residuals (`observed - predicted`)

What you want to see:

- A random cloud of points around 0
- No clear curve pattern
- Similar vertical spread across the full x-range

What can indicate a problem:

- Curved pattern: the relationship may not be linear
- Funnel shape (narrow on one side, wide on the other): non-constant variance
- A few points far away from the rest: possible influential outliers to investigate

This plot is not a "pass/fail" test by itself. Use it as a quick visual check before interpreting slope, intercept, and predictions.

Starter diagnostic example:

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance = c(0.003, 0.057, 0.110, 0.226, 0.441, 0.889)
)

model <- lm(absorbance ~ conc_ug_ml, data = calibration)

# Residuals vs fitted values (first diagnostic view)
plot(model, which = 1)
```

</div>
</details>
